Use strict expression validation together with a restricted evaluator. The returned security tool produced an assessment prompt template; it did not audit your code or verify an expression.

For your Python codebase:

- Avoid `eval()` and `exec()` for untrusted input. Use a mathematical parser with an explicit allowlist of numeric literals, operators, functions, and permitted variable names.
- Reject attribute access, imports, arbitrary calls, and all unsupported syntax. Validate and evaluate with the same grammar.
- With the supplied math tools, use `validate_syntax(expression=..., detailed=True, allow_variables=False)` for syntax checking, or `evaluate(expression=..., validate_only=True)` before evaluation. Syntax validity alone does not establish safe execution.
- Limit input length, nesting, operation count, numeric magnitude, and exponent size. Enforce time and memory limits in an isolated worker.
- Handle division by zero, domain errors, overflow, and non-finite results with controlled errors. Keep variable contexts isolated between users and requests.
- Test permitted arithmetic, malformed input, attempted Python execution, excessive nesting, huge powers, and cross-user variable access. Rate-limit requests, monitor rejected inputs without logging sensitive data, and audit dependencies.

These controls follow OWASP input-validation and injection-prevention principles. References: [Input Validation Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html) and [Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html).

No specific expression or implementation was supplied, so none has been directly validated.
